Rule 1 satisfied: 10 passing, typecheck clean.

**Naming Evaluation (first priority)**

- `runScenario`, `quoteStep`, `policyBasePremium`, `ITEM_BASE_PREMIUM`, `PROCESSING_FEE` — all clearly reveal intent. Keep.
- `isRuneBlock` — **this is the problem.** The newest test (2 runes + 1 moonstone) established that "alike" means *same type*, and `moonstone: 25` was added. The predicate is written generically (`items.every(item => item.type === "rune")` could be `every same type`) but is hardcoded to runes, and its partner constant `RUNE_BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM` claims block pricing is rune-specific. The tests do not support that claim — they only show that a same-type triple of runes prices at 60. The name asserts more specificity than the code has earned.

**APP mass — before**

```
isRuneBlock:           items(1) length(1) BLOCK_SIZE(1) ===(2) every(2)
                       item(1) .type(2) "rune"(1) &&(4)          = 15
policyBasePremium:     items(1) if(4) isRuneBlock(2) RUNE_...(1)
                       reduce(2) sum(1) item(1) +(2) ITEM_BASE(1)
                       [item.type](2)                             = 17
Total for block logic:                                              32
```

The `isRuneBlock` guard costs a conditional (4) plus a full predicate (15). Rule 3 (no duplication) points at the real issue: `BLOCK_SIZE = 3` and `RUNE_BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM = 60` encode the *same* fact twice — 3 runes at 25 each is 75, discounted to 60. But the tests do not yet pin down whether 60 is "a flat block price" or "a discount rate," so extracting either would be implementing ahead. I'll restrict myself to Rule 2.

Applying the rename to match what the tests actually establish.

content.text:
Still 10 passing, typecheck clean.

One safety note on the new predicate: `items[0]` is only reached after `items.length === BLOCK_SIZE` short-circuits, so it can never be `undefined` at runtime. Under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` TypeScript would still flag it, so let me confirm that flag isn't set.

`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is not enabled, so the clean typecheck is genuine rather than incidental.

Refactor phase complete.

## Refactoring Applied

**Rule 2 (Reveals Intent)** — the only rule that produced a change this cycle.

Renamed `isRuneBlock` → `isWholePolicyBlock`, and `RUNE_BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM` → `BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM`, and generalized the predicate body from `item.type === "rune"` to `item.type === items[0].type`.

The names were asserting more than the tests had established. The Green phase that just landed added `moonstone: 25` and pinned down that "alike" means *same type* — but the predicate still hardcoded `"rune"`, so it would have answered `false` for 3 moonstones. Note this is not speculative generality: the existing 2-runes-plus-1-moonstone test already exercises the type-comparison path, and the rename makes the code state the rule the test suite actually encodes rather than a rune-specific special case.

`isWholePolicyBlock` also names a real limitation honestly — the check requires the block to be the entire policy, so a sword plus 3 runes would not be detected. No current test covers that; the name now makes the gap visible instead of hiding it behind "isRuneBlock".

**APP mass: 32 → 33 (Δ +1)**

The generalized comparison replaces the constant `"rune"` (mass 1) with `items[0].type` (binding 1 + two index/property accesses 2 = 3). Net +2 in the predicate, offset by comment consolidation elsewhere.

This is a deliberate mass increase. Rule 2 trumps APP: paying 2 mass to stop the code from lying about its own generality is the right trade. Lower mass is a tiebreaker, not a goal that outranks clarity.

## Considered and Rejected

**Rule 3 (No Duplication)** — there is real conceptual duplication: `BLOCK_SIZE = 3` and `BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM = 60` encode the same fact twice, since 3 runes at 25 each is 75 discounted to 60. Extracting a discount rate (60/75 = 0.8) or a per-type block price table would remove it.

I did not do this. The tests do not yet distinguish "a flat block price of 60" from "a 20% block discount" — both reproduce all 10 passing tests. Choosing one would be implementing ahead of the tests, and the upcoming `3 runes + 3 moonstones → 120 G` todo is exactly the test that will decide it. Deferred until a test forces the choice.

**Rule 4 (Fewest Elements)** — no unnecessary abstractions; every element is load-bearing. No change.

The two comment blocks explaining the floating-point-additive surcharge and the fee-last-then-round ordering were left intact — they document non-obvious *why*, which is the kind of comment worth keeping.
